### Problem `#069` — Luogu P4174 [NOI2006]: 最大获利 (Maximum Profit)

- **Canonical Slot**: `Ch 09 — Advanced 1 (Adv-1)` | **Judge URL**: [Luogu P4174](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P4174) *(Judge Mirrors: `BZOJ 1497`, [SPOJ PROFIT](https://www.spoj.com/problems/PROFIT/))*
- **Constraints**: $1 \le N \le 5000$ base stations, $1 \le M \le 5 \cdot 10^4$ user demand groups; station build costs $P_i \in [1, 100]$, demand revenues $C_k \in [1, 100]$; Time Limit $1.0\text{ s}$.
- **Problem Statement**: A telecom company can build any subset of $N$ candidate cell towers, where building tower $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ costs $P_i > 0$. There are $M$ user demand groups: group $k \in \{1, \dots, M\}$ requires **both** tower $a_k$ and tower $b_k$ to be built, and if both are built, the company earns revenue $C_k > 0$. Maximize the company's net profit (total revenue minus total tower construction cost).

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Why Pairwise Conjunction Needs an Auxiliary Hub (or Vertex-Edge Merging)"}
If you try to connect $a_k$ and $b_k$ directly without an auxiliary vertex, how do you represent $+C_k x_{a_k} x_{b_k}$? In this chapter, the most transparent method is to introduce an auxiliary binary variable $z_k \in \{0, 1\}$ for demand group $k$ with the closure implications $z_k = 1 \implies x_{a_k} = 1$ and $z_k = 1 \implies x_{b_k} = 1$. *(Note: When $M = \Theta(N^2)$ is a dense matrix as in `[TJOI2015] 线性代数` (`Luogu P3973`), we can eliminate the $M$ auxiliary vertices entirely via the identity $1 - x_i x_j = (1 - x_i) + x_i(1 - x_j)$, which we formalize in `Chapter 10`!)*
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Bipartite Closure Network & Dinic Complexity"}
Wire $S \xrightarrow{C_k} \text{User}_k$, $\text{User}_k \xrightarrow{+\infty} \text{Tower}_{a_k}$, $\text{User}_k \xrightarrow{+\infty} \text{Tower}_{b_k}$, and $\text{Tower}_i \xrightarrow{P_i} T$. Even though $|V| = N + M + 2 \le 55,002$ and $|E| = 3M + N \le 155,000$, this is a **2-layer bipartite closure network**, on which Dinic runs in $O(M\sqrt{N})$ time ($< 40\text{ ms}$)!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Constant-Factor Orientation Tip (`S -> Tower -> User -> T`)"}
In Dinic's DFS, each user node $\text{User}_k$ has out-degree $2$ (pointing to $a_k, b_k$), whereas in the transposed network $S \xrightarrow{P_i} \text{Tower}_i \xrightarrow{+\infty} \text{User}_k \xrightarrow{C_k} T$, each $\text{User}_k$ has out-degree $1$ (pointing only to $T$). Both orientations have the exact same minimum cut and pass well within $50\text{ ms}$.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & C++ Solution — #069 (Luogu P4174 — Maximum Profit)"}
#### Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
We must choose a subset of $N \le 5000$ cost-bearing stations to satisfy a subset of $M \le 5 \cdot 10^4$ positive-revenue pair demands $(a_k, b_k, C_k)$. This is the large-scale benchmark for **Bipartite Pair-Hub Closure** (mathematically identical to `#067 Petya and Graph`, scaled up $50\times$ to test $O(M\sqrt{N})$ Dinic efficiency).

#### Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Let $x_i = [\text{Tower } i \text{ built}] \in \{0, 1\}$ and $z_k = [\text{User } k \text{ served}] \in \{0, 1\}$:

$$\max_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}} \left(\sum_{k=1}^M C_k z_k - \sum_{i=1}^N P_i x_i\right) = \sum_{k=1}^M C_k - \min_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}} \left(\sum_{k=1}^M C_k(1 - z_k) + \sum_{i=1}^N P_i x_i + \sum_{k=1}^M \infty\big(z_k(1 - x_{a_k}) + z_k(1 - x_{b_k})\big)\right).$$

#### Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)
- Vertices: $S = 0$, towers $1 \dots N$, users $N + 1 \dots N + M$, $T = N + M + 1$.
- For each tower $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$: wire $i \xrightarrow{P_i} T$.
- For each demand $k \in \{1, \dots, M\}$: add $C_k$ to $W^+$, wire $S \xrightarrow{C_k} (N + k)$, $(N + k) \xrightarrow{+\infty} a_k$, and $(N + k) \xrightarrow{+\infty} b_k$.
- Output $W^+ - \text{MaxFlow}(S, T)$.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Dense-Matrix Alternative Preview
- **Toy Trace**: $N = 3$ towers with $P = (3, 4, 5)$; $M = 2$ users: $(1, 2, C_1 = 6)$ and $(2, 3, C_2 = 6)$.
  - Baseline $W^+ = 6 + 6 = 12$.
  - Building $\{1, 2\}$ gives $6 - (3 + 4) = -1 < 0$; building $\{2, 3\}$ gives $6 - (4 + 5) = -3 < 0$.
  - Building all three $\{1, 2, 3\}$ shares Tower $2$'s cost $P_2 = 4$, giving $(6 + 6) - (3 + 4 + 5) = 12 - 12 = 0$.
  - What if $C_1 = 7, C_2 = 7$? Then $W^+ = 14$, cutting $(1 \to T, 3), (2 \to T, 4), (3 \to T, 5)$ costs $12$, yielding $14 - 12 = \mathbf{2}$.
- **Failure-Mode Guard (Sparse vs. Dense Pairwise Closure)**: Here $M = 5 \cdot 10^4$ is sparse compared to $\binom{5000}{2} \approx 1.25 \cdot 10^7$, so creating $M$ auxiliary vertices is optimal. By contrast, in **`[TJOI2015] 线性代数` (`Luogu P3973`)**, where we maximize $\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^N B_{i,j} x_i x_j - \sum_{i=1}^N C_i x_i$ for a **dense** $500 \times 500$ matrix $B_{i,j} \ge 0$, creating $N^2 = 2.5 \cdot 10^5$ auxiliary vertices is unnecessary: using $x_i - x_i x_j = x_i(1 - x_j)$, we wire $S \xrightarrow{\sum_j B_{i,j}} i$, $i \xrightarrow{C_i} T$, and $i \xrightarrow{B_{i,j}} j$ on just **$N = 500$ vertices**!

```cpp
// Complete Model Compilation for #069 (Luogu P4174 — [NOI2006] Maximum Profit)
long long solve_maximum_profit(int N, int M, const vector<int>& P,
                               const vector<tuple<int, int, int>>& demands) {
    int S = 0, T = N + M + 1;
    const long long INF = 1e15;
    Dinic<long long> dinic(T + 1, S, T);
    long long W_plus = 0;

    for (int i = 1; i <= N; ++i) {
        dinic.add_edge(i, T, P[i - 1]);
    }
    for (int k = 1; k <= M; ++k) {
        auto [a, b, c] = demands[k - 1];
        W_plus += c;
        dinic.add_edge(S, N + k, c);
        dinic.add_edge(N + k, a, INF);
        dinic.add_edge(N + k, b, INF);
    }
    return W_plus - dinic.max_flow();
}
```

### Problem `#070` — Luogu P2805 [NOI2009]: 植物大战僵尸 (Plants vs. Zombies)

- **Canonical Slot**: `Ch 09 — Advanced 2 (Adv-2)` | **Judge URL**: [Luogu P2805](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P2805)
- **Constraints**: Grid dimensions $1 \le N \le 20$ rows, $1 \le M \le 30$ columns ($N M \le 600$ cells); plant scores $w_{r,c} \in [-10^4, 10^4]$; Time Limit $1.0\text{ s}$.
- **Problem Statement**: A lawn is an $N \times M$ grid ($0$-indexed rows $0 \dots N-1$ and columns $0 \dots M-1$). Each cell $(r, c)$ contains a plant with signed score $w_{r,c} \in \mathbb{Z}$ (eating it grants $w_{r,c}$ points; negative means eating it costs points) and a list of target cells $(r_1, c_1), \dots, (r_k, c_k)$ that plant $(r, c)$ attacks/protects.
  - Zombies can only enter each row from the **right border** (column $M - 1$) and advance leftward: to eat plant $(r, c)$, zombies must first eat all plants $(r, c + 1), (r, c + 2), \dots, (r, M - 1)$ to its right in the same row.
  - Furthermore, if plant $v$ attacks cell $u$, any zombie stepping onto cell $u$ is instantly destroyed unless plant $v$ has **already been eaten**!
  Choose a valid sequential eating strategy to maximize the total score of eaten plants.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Building the Complete Causal Prerequisite Graph $G_{\text{pre}}$"}
What are ALL the prerequisites that must be eaten *before* cell $u = (r, c)$ can be eaten?
1. If $c + 1 < M$, cell $(r, c + 1)$ must be eaten before $(r, c)$: add $(r, c + 1) \xrightarrow{\text{unlocks}} (r, c)$ to $G_{\text{pre}}$.
2. If plant $v$ attacks cell $u$, then $v$ must be eaten before $u$: add $v \xrightarrow{\text{unlocks}} u$ to $G_{\text{pre}}$.
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Eliminating Cyclic Deadlocks via Kahn's Topological Sort (`FM-09`)"}
Why can't we run Picard's closure directly on $G_{\text{pre}}$? Because of **Broken-Gadget Counterexample `FM-09` (`Section 3.2`)**: if two plants protect each other in a cycle (or if a row dependency and an attack edge form a cycle $(r, c+1) \to (r, c) \to (r, c+1)$), neither plant can ever be eaten first, AND any plant causally downstream of that cycle is also permanently invincible! Run **Kahn's in-degree-$0$ BFS** on $G_{\text{pre}}$ first!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Reversing Surviving Edges for the Picard Closure Network"}
Only vertices visited by Kahn's BFS (`vis_kahn[u] == true`) are physically eatable. On those surviving vertices, if $(v \xrightarrow{\text{unlocks}} u) \in E_{\text{pre}}$, then eating $u$ ($x_u = 1$) requires eating $v$ ($x_v = 1$), so you wire the **reversed** edge $u \xrightarrow{+\infty} v$ in Dinic!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & C++ Solution — #070 (Luogu P2805 — Plants vs. Zombies)"}
#### Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
This is the definitive benchmark for **Sequential Causal Closure (`Semantics B`, Section 3)**: eating a plant requires eating its right-hand row neighbor and all of its protectors first, and cycles in the prerequisite graph cause permanent physical deadlock (`FM-09`).

#### Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Let $U = \{0, \dots, NM - 1\}$ where cell $(r, c)$ has ID $u = r M + c$.
1. **Causal Graph $G_{\text{pre}} = (U, E_{\text{pre}})$**: $(v \to u) \in E_{\text{pre}}$ iff $v$ must be eaten before $u$.
2. **Reachability Filter**: $U_{\text{valid}} \subseteq U$ is the set of vertices popped during Kahn's topological sort on $G_{\text{pre}}$.
3. **Closure Optimization on $U_{\text{valid}}$**: Let $x_u = [u \text{ eaten}] \in \{0, 1\}$ for $u \in U_{\text{valid}}$. Then $(v \to u) \in E_{\text{pre}}(U_{\text{valid}})$ enforces $x_u = 1 \implies x_v = 1$, compiled as $\infty \cdot x_u(1 - x_v)$ ($u \xrightarrow{+\infty} v$).

#### Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)
- Map $(r, c) \mapsto u = r M + c \in [0, NM - 1]$.
- For each cell $u = (r, c)$:
  - If $c + 1 < M$, add directed edge $(r M + c + 1) \to u$ to $G_{\text{pre}}$.
  - For each target cell $(tr, tc)$ attacked by $u$, add directed edge $u \to (tr \cdot M + tc)$ to $G_{\text{pre}}$.
- Run Kahn's BFS on $G_{\text{pre}}$ using `in_deg[0 .. NM-1]` to compute `valid[0 .. NM-1]`.
- Build $\mathcal{N}$ on $NM + 2$ vertices ($S = NM, T = NM + 1$):
  - For each $u$ with `valid[u] == true`:
    - If $w_u > 0$: add $w_u$ to $W^+$ and wire $S \xrightarrow{w_u} u$.
    - If $w_u < 0$: wire $u \xrightarrow{-w_u} T$.
    - For each $(v \to u) \in E_{\text{pre}}$ with `valid[v] == true`: wire $u \xrightarrow{+\infty} v$.
- Output $W^+ - \text{MaxFlow}(S, T)$.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
- **Toy Trace**: See **Section 3.2 (`FM-09`)**, where $u_2 \leftrightarrow u_3$ deadlocks and blocks $u_1$ ($w(u_1) = +1000$). Kahn's BFS visits only $u_4$, outputting $+50$ instead of the unpruned $+1030$ or the Tarjan-SCC $+1050$.
- **Failure-Mode Guard**: Double-check the direction of both edges:
  1. In $G_{\text{pre}}$ (Kahn's BFS): `protector -> protected` and `(r, c+1) -> (r, c)`.
  2. In $\mathcal{N}$ (Dinic): `protected -> protector` and `(r, c) -> (r, c+1)` with capacity $+\infty$.

```cpp
// Complete Two-Phase Causal Pruning + Closure Solver for #070 (Luogu P2805)
long long solve_pvz(int N, int M, const vector<long long>& score,
                    const vector<vector<int>>& attacks) {
    int V = N * M;
    vector<vector<int>> adj_pre(V);
    vector<int> in_deg(V, 0);

    auto add_pre = [&](int protector, int target) {
        adj_pre[protector].push_back(target);
        in_deg[target]++;
    };

    for (int r = 0; r < N; ++r) {
        for (int c = 0; c < M; ++c) {
            int u = r * M + c;
            if (c + 1 < M) {
                add_pre(r * M + (c + 1), u); // must eat (r, c+1) before (r, c)
            }
            for (int target : attacks[u]) {
                add_pre(u, target); // u protects target -> must eat u before target
            }
        }
    }

    // Phase 1: Kahn's Topological BFS on G_pre to prune cycles and their descendants
    vector<bool> valid(V, false);
    queue<int> q;
    for (int u = 0; u < V; ++u) {
        if (in_deg[u] == 0) q.push(u);
    }
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int u = q.front();
        q.pop();
        valid[u] = true;
        for (int nxt : adj_pre[u]) {
            if (--in_deg[nxt] == 0) q.push(nxt);
        }
    }

    // Phase 2: Build Picard Closure Network ONLY on Kahn-validated vertices
    int S = V, T = V + 1;
    const long long INF = 1e15;
    Dinic<long long> dinic(V + 2, S, T);
    long long W_plus = 0;

    for (int u = 0; u < V; ++u) {
        if (!valid[u]) continue;
        if (score[u] > 0) {
            W_plus += score[u];
            dinic.add_edge(S, u, score[u]);
        } else if (score[u] < 0) {
            dinic.add_edge(u, T, -score[u]);
        }
        for (int nxt : adj_pre[u]) {
            if (valid[nxt]) {
                // Eating nxt requires eating u -> closure edge nxt -> u of cap INF
                dinic.add_edge(nxt, u, INF);
            }
        }
    }
    return W_plus - dinic.max_flow();
}
```

### Problem `#071` — Luogu P3749 [SHOI2017]: 寿司餐厅 (Sushi Restaurant)

- **Canonical Slot**: `Ch 09 — Mastery 1 (Mas-1)` | **Judge URL**: [Luogu P3749 (`[六省联考2017]`)](https://www.luogu.com.cn/problem/P3749)
- **Constraints**: $1 \le N \le 100$ sushi plates, $m \in \{0, 1\}$, sushi type codes $1 \le a_i \le 1000$, interval scores $d_{l,r} \in [-10^3, 10^3]$; Time Limit $1.0\text{ s}$.
- **Problem Statement**: A conveyor belt holds $N$ sushi plates in a row, where plate $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ has sushi type $a_i$.
  - If you choose to eat a contiguous interval of plates $[l, r]$ ($1 \le l \le r \le N$), you automatically select **all** sub-intervals $[l', r'] \subseteq [l, r]$ as well. Each selected interval $[l, r]$ grants a signed satisfaction score $d_{l,r} \in \mathbb{Z}$ (counted at most once even if covered by multiple larger intervals).
  - If you eat $c \ge 1$ plates of sushi type $x$ in total, you must pay a sushi bill of $m x^2 + c x$.
  Maximize the net profit (total satisfaction score minus total sushi bill).

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Compressing Interval Inclusion to a 2-Out-Degree Pyramid (`Section 4.2`)"}
Treat each interval $[l, r]$ ($1 \le l \le r \le N$) as a vertex in the closure graph. Since $[l, r] \implies [l + 1, r]$ and $[l, r] \implies [l, r - 1]$ transitively generate every sub-interval $[l', r'] \subseteq [l, r]$, you only need **two** $\infty$-edges out of each $[l, r]$ ($l < r$)!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Splitting $m x^2 + c x$ into Per-Plate and Per-Type Costs"}
When is plate $i$ physically eaten? Precisely when the length-$1$ interval $[i, i]$ is selected!
- The linear cost $c \cdot x = \sum_{i \text{ eaten}} a_i$ charges $a_i$ once for each eaten plate $i$: simply set the net weight of node $[i, i]$ to $w_{i,i} = d_{i,i} - a_i$!
- The quadratic cost $m \cdot x^2$ is paid **once** per distinct sushi type $x$ if at least one plate of type $x$ is eaten: create a type hub $\text{Type}_x$ with edge $\text{Type}_x \xrightarrow{m x^2} T$, and wire $[i, i] \xrightarrow{+\infty} \text{Type}_{a_i}$!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Vertex & Edge Budget Check"}
There are $\binom{N+1}{2} \le 5050$ interval vertices and $\le 1000$ type vertices ($\le 6052$ vertices total), with $\le 15,000$ directed edges. Dinic solves this network in $< 15\text{ ms}$.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & C++ Solution — #071 (Luogu P3749 — Sushi Restaurant)"}
#### Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
Contiguous interval inclusion ($[l, r]$ forces all sub-intervals $[l', r'] \subseteq [l, r]$) combined with overlapping global item-type taxes $m x^2$ breaks interval DP (`dp[l][r]` cannot merge two intervals without double-counting shared sushi types $x$ or overlapping sub-intervals). This is the canonical **Interval-Triangle Pyramid Closure (`Section 4.2`)**.

#### Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Let $x_{l,r} \in \{0, 1\}$ indicate selecting interval $[l, r]$ ($1 \le l \le r \le N$), and let $y_v \in \{0, 1\}$ indicate activating sushi type $v \in \{1, \dots, 1000\}$. Define modified interval weights:

$$\tilde{w}_{l,r} = \begin{cases} d_{l,r} & \text{if } l < r, \\ d_{i,i} - a_i & \text{if } l = r = i. \end{cases}$$

We maximize:

$$\max_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}} \left(\sum_{1 \le l \le r \le N} \tilde{w}_{l,r} x_{l,r} - \sum_{v=1}^{1000} m v^2 y_v\right) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \begin{cases} x_{l,r} \le x_{l+1,r} \;\land\; x_{l,r} \le x_{l,r-1} & (1 \le l < r \le N), \\ x_{i,i} \le y_{a_i} & (1 \le i \le N). \end{cases}$$

#### Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)
- Assign unique node IDs `id[l][r]` for $1 \le l \le r \le N$ ($1 \dots \binom{N+1}{2}$) and `type_id[v]` for each distinct sushi type $v$ present in $a_1, \dots, a_N$.
- For each interval $[l, r]$:
  - If $\tilde{w}_{l,r} > 0$: add $\tilde{w}_{l,r}$ to $W^+$ and wire $S \xrightarrow{\tilde{w}_{l,r}} \text{id}[l][r]$.
  - If $\tilde{w}_{l,r} < 0$: wire $\text{id}[l][r] \xrightarrow{-\tilde{w}_{l,r}} T$.
  - If $l < r$: wire $\text{id}[l][r] \xrightarrow{+\infty} \text{id}[l+1][r]$ and $\text{id}[l][r] \xrightarrow{+\infty} \text{id}[l][r-1]$.
  - If $l = r$: wire $\text{id}[l][l] \xrightarrow{+\infty} \text{type\_id}[a_l]$.
- For each distinct sushi type $v$: if $m = 1$, wire $\text{type\_id}[v] \xrightarrow{v^2} T$.
- Output $W^+ - \text{MaxFlow}(S, T)$.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
- **Toy Trace**: $N = 2, m = 1$, types $a = [2, 2]$. Scores: $d_{1,1} = 5, d_{2,2} = 5, d_{1,2} = -1$.
  - Singleton net weights: $\tilde{w}_{1,1} = 5 - 2 = +3$, $\tilde{w}_{2,2} = 5 - 2 = +3$; pair weight $\tilde{w}_{1,2} = -1$.
  - Type hub $\text{Type}_2$ has cost $1 \cdot 2^2 = 4$ ($\text{Type}_2 \xrightarrow{4} T$).
  - Since $[1, 1] \to \text{Type}_2$ and $[2, 2] \to \text{Type}_2$ share the single type hub, choosing $\{[1, 1], [2, 2], \text{Type}_2\}$ (without choosing $[1, 2]$!) gains $3 + 3 - 4 = \mathbf{2}$!
  - Notice that eating plate $1$ and plate $2$ individually does **not** force eating the interval $[1, 2]$ (whose implication $[1, 2] \to [1, 1], [2, 2]$ points downward, not upward!).
- **Failure-Mode Guard**: Never add reverse edges $[l+1, r] \land [l, r-1] \implies [l, r]$! The problem statement says choosing $[l, r]$ includes sub-intervals of $[l, r]$; eating $[1, 1]$ and $[2, 2]$ separately does NOT force you to take a negative $d_{1,2} < 0$!

```cpp
// Complete Model Compilation for #071 (Luogu P3749 — [SHOI2017] Sushi Restaurant)
long long solve_sushi_restaurant(int N, int m, const vector<int>& a,
                                 const vector<vector<long long>>& d) {
    vector<vector<int>> id(N + 1, vector<int>(N + 1, 0));
    int node_cnt = 0;
    for (int l = 1; l <= N; ++l)
        for (int r = l; r <= N; ++r)
            id[l][r] = ++node_cnt;

    int max_a = *max_element(a.begin(), a.end());
    vector<int> type_id(max_a + 1, 0);
    for (int x : a) {
        if (!type_id[x]) type_id[x] = ++node_cnt;
    }

    int S = 0, T = node_cnt + 1;
    const long long INF = 1e15;
    Dinic<long long> dinic(T + 1, S, T);
    long long W_plus = 0;

    for (int l = 1; l <= N; ++l) {
        for (int r = l; r <= N; ++r) {
            long long w = d[l][r] - (l == r ? a[l - 1] : 0);
            if (w > 0) {
                W_plus += w;
                dinic.add_edge(S, id[l][r], w);
            } else if (w < 0) {
                dinic.add_edge(id[l][r], T, -w);
            }
            if (l < r) {
                dinic.add_edge(id[l][r], id[l + 1][r], INF);
                dinic.add_edge(id[l][r], id[l][r - 1], INF);
            } else {
                dinic.add_edge(id[l][l], type_id[a[l - 1]], INF);
            }
        }
    }
    if (m == 1) {
        for (int x = 1; x <= max_a; ++x) {
            if (type_id[x]) {
                dinic.add_edge(type_id[x], T, 1LL * x * x);
            }
        }
    }
    return W_plus - dinic.max_flow();
}
```

### Problem `#072` — Codeforces 103 E: Buying Sets

- **Canonical Slot**: `Ch 09 — Mastery 2 (Mas-2)` | **Judge URL**: [Codeforces 103 E](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/103/E)
- **Constraints**: $1 \le N \le 300$ sets over universe $\{1, \dots, N\}$, set purchase costs $w_i \in [-10^6, 10^6]$; Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$.
- **Problem Statement**: You are given $N$ subsets $A_1, \dots, A_N \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$, where buying set $A_i$ costs $w_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ (if $w_i < 0$, buying $A_i$ earns $-w_i$ profit). It is guaranteed that for every $k \in \{1, \dots, N\}$, the union of any $k$ subsets contains **at least $k$ elements** ($\big|\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\big| \ge |I|$). Find a subcollection of sets $I \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ whose union contains **exactly $|I|$ elements** ($\big|\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\big| = |I|$) that minimizes the total cost $\sum_{i \in I} w_i$ (note that $I = \emptyset$ is valid with cost $0$).

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Exploiting the Hall Guarantee $|N(I)| \ge |I|$"}
Because *every* subcollection $I \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}$ satisfies $|N(I)| \ge |I|$, the excess $|N(I)| - |I|$ is **always non-negative** ($\ge 0$), and equals $0$ if and only if $|N(I)| = |I|$!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Method 1: Uniform Pedestal Shift `+M` (`ゲタを履かせる`)"}
As derived in **Section 4.3**, set $M = 10^9 > N \max |w_i| = 3 \cdot 10^8$. Give each set $i$ a positive closure weight $M - w_i > 0$ ($S \xrightarrow{M - w_i} \text{Set}_i$), each element $j \in \{1, \dots, N\}$ a negative closure weight $-M$ ($\text{Elem}_j \xrightarrow{M} T$), and wire $\text{Set}_i \xrightarrow{+\infty} \text{Elem}_j$ for all $j \in A_i$. Then any closed set $(I, J)$ has weight $-(|J| - |I|)M - \sum_{i \in I} w_i$, which is forced to have $|J| = |N(I)| = |I|$!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Method 2: Hall Perfect Matching + $N$-Vertex Closure"}
Alternatively, find a perfect matching $M(i) \in A_i$ first, and wire $i \xrightarrow{+\infty} M^{-1}(e)$ for all $e \in A_i$ on an $N$-vertex closure network with weights $-w_i$ (`Section 4.3 Method 2`). Both methods run in $< 15\text{ ms}$!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & C++ Solution — #072 (Codeforces 103 E — Buying Sets)"}
#### Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
"Union of $k$ sets has size $\ge k$ for all $k$" is the verbatim statement of **Hall's Marriage Condition** (`Chapter 8`). Combining Hall's non-negative excess $|N(I)| - |I| \ge 0$ with an exact-equality requirement $|N(I)| = |I|$ and signed set costs $w_i$ triggers **Hall-Shifted Bipartite Closure (`Section 4.3`)**.

#### Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation (`+M` Pedestal Shift)
Let $x_i = [i \in I] \in \{0, 1\}$ for sets and $y_j = [j \in J] \in \{0, 1\}$ for elements, with $M = 10^9$:

$$\max_{\substack{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \{0,1\}^N \\ x_i \le y_j \; (\forall j \in A_i)}} \left(\sum_{i=1}^N (M - w_i) x_i - \sum_{j=1}^N M y_j\right) = \sum_{i=1}^N (M - w_i) - \text{MinCut}(S, T).$$

Since $\max \text{Closure} = \max_{|N(I)| = |I|} \sum_{i \in I} (-w_i) = -\min_{|N(I)| = |I|} \sum_{i \in I} w_i$, the minimum cost $\sum_{i \in I^*} w_i$ is simply:

$$\min_{|N(I)| = |I|} \sum_{i \in I} w_i = \text{MinCut}(S, T) - \sum_{i=1}^N (M - w_i).$$

#### Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)
- Set $M = 10^9$, `INF = 1e16`.
- Vertices: $S = 0$, sets $1 \dots N$, elements $N + 1 \dots 2N$, $T = 2N + 1$.
- For each set $i \in \{1, \dots, N\}$:
  - Add $M - w_i$ to $W^+$; wire $S \xrightarrow{M - w_i} i$.
  - For each element $j \in A_i$: wire $i \xrightarrow{+\infty} (N + j)$.
- For each element $j \in \{1, \dots, N\}$: wire $(N + j) \xrightarrow{M} T$.
- Output $\text{MaxFlow}(S, T) - W^+$.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
- **Toy Trace ($N = 3$)**:
  - $A_1 = \{1, 2\}$ ($w_1 = -10$), $A_2 = \{2, 3\}$ ($w_2 = +4$), $A_3 = \{3\}$ ($w_3 = -5$).
  - Check all subsets $I$ with $|N(I)| = |I|$:
    - $I = \emptyset \implies \text{cost } 0$.
    - $I = \{1\} \implies N(\{1\}) = \{1, 2\}$ (size $2 > 1$, invalid!).
    - $I = \{3\} \implies N(\{3\}) = \{3\}$ (size $1 = 1$, valid, cost $-5$).
    - $I = \{2, 3\} \implies N(\{2, 3\}) = \{2, 3\}$ (size $2 = 2$, valid, cost $4 - 5 = -1$).
    - $I = \{1, 2, 3\} \implies N(\{1, 2, 3\}) = \{1, 2, 3\}$ (size $3 = 3$, valid, cost $-10 + 4 - 5 = \mathbf{-11}$).
  - With $M = 100$: set weights are $W_1 = 110, W_2 = 96, W_3 = 105$ ($W^+ = 311$), element costs are $100$ each.
  - Choosing $I = \{1\}$ ($J = \{1, 2\}$) gives $110 - 200 = -90 < 0$ (rejected!).
  - Choosing $I = \{1, 2, 3\}$ ($J = \{1, 2, 3\}$) severs the three element edges to $T$ (cut $= 300$), giving $\text{MinCut} - W^+ = 300 - 311 = \mathbf{-11}$!
- **Failure-Mode Guard**: In the $+M$ pedestal method, $M$ **must** strictly exceed $N \cdot \max_i |w_i| = 300 \times 10^6 = 3 \cdot 10^8$ (so $M = 10^9$ is safe, whereas $M = 10^7$ fails when $300$ sets each have $w_i = -10^6$). And because $N \cdot M = 3 \cdot 10^{11}$, all capacities and flow variables must be `long long`!

```cpp
// Complete Model Compilation for #072 (Codeforces 103 E — Buying Sets) via +M Pedestal Shift
long long solve_buying_sets(int N, const vector<vector<int>>& sets,
                            const vector<long long>& w) {
    int S = 0, T = 2 * N + 1;
    const long long M_PEDESTAL = 1e9; // > N * max|w_i| = 3e8
    const long long INF = 1e16;
    Dinic<long long> dinic(T + 1, S, T);
    long long W_plus = 0;

    for (int i = 1; i <= N; ++i) {
        long long cap_s = M_PEDESTAL - w[i - 1];
        W_plus += cap_s;
        dinic.add_edge(S, i, cap_s);
        for (int elem : sets[i - 1]) {
            dinic.add_edge(i, N + elem, INF);
        }
    }
    for (int j = 1; j <= N; ++j) {
        dinic.add_edge(N + j, T, M_PEDESTAL);
    }
    // Minimum cost = -(W_plus - min_cut) = min_cut - W_plus
    return dinic.max_flow() - W_plus;
}
```
::::

## 7. Pre-Submission Verification Checklist (`FM-09` Audit)

Before submitting any Binary Assignment, Project Selection, or Maximum-Weight Closure solution, audit your code against these six failure-mode guards:

1. **Sequential vs. Simultaneous Cycle Semantics (`FM-09` / `[NOI2009] 植物大战僵尸`)**:
   - Does the problem require a valid sequential unlocking order (`Semantics B`)?
   - If **yes**, did you run **Kahn's in-degree-$0$ BFS** on the causal graph $G_{\text{pre}}$ (`protector -> protected`) and discard all unvisited vertices *before* building the flow network? (Never use Tarjan's SCC deletion `|SCC| >= 2`, which fails to prune acyclic vertices downstream of a cycle!)
2. **Implication Arc Orientation (`x_u = 1 => x_v = 1`)**:
   - Under Convention A ($x_u = 1 \iff u \in V_S$, where $S \xrightarrow{w_u} u$ for $w_u > 0$ and $v \xrightarrow{|w_v|} T$ for $w_v < 0$), the forbidden state is $(u \in V_S, v \in V_T)$, so the $\infty$-arc **always** points from dependent to prerequisite: $u \xrightarrow{+\infty} v$.
   - Did you verify on a 2-vertex trace (like Gem $1$ and Gem $2$ in `ARC 085 E`) that the legal asymmetric state crosses backward from $V_T$ to $V_S$ (cost $0$) while the illegal state crosses forward from $V_S$ to $V_T$ (cost $+\infty$)?
3. **Constructive Closure Extraction (`S_min` vs. Single-Edge Saturation)**:
   - When reconstructing the chosen subset $C^*$ (`Luogu P2762`, `POJ 2987`), did you run a residual BFS from $S$ traversing edges with `cap - flow > 0` (`get_S_min()`) instead of checking whether individual $S \to u$ or $v \to T$ edges are saturated?
4. **Optimistic Baseline Inclusion (`W^+` Sum)**:
   - Did you add **only strictly positive** weights ($w_u > 0$) into $W^+$?
   - For singleton intervals with linear costs (like $\tilde{w}_{i,i} = d_{i,i} - a_i$ in `[SHOI2017] 寿司餐厅`), did you compute the net weight $\tilde{w}_{i,i}$ **first**, and only then test `if (w > 0)` vs. `if (w < 0)`?
5. **Transitive DAG Sparsification**:
   - In interval inclusion (`寿司餐厅`) or divisibility posets (`ARC 085 E`), did you wire only Hasse/adjacent transitions ($[l, r] \to [l+1, r], [l, r-1]$) instead of all $O(N^4)$ sub-interval pairs?
6. **64-Bit Integer Overflow Guard**:
   - Is `INF` strictly greater than $W^+ = \sum_{w_u > 0} w_u$ (e.g., `INF = 1e16` in `long long`), while still satisfying `INF + INF < LLONG_MAX`?

---

## 8. Chapter Summary & Bridge to Chapter 10

### Key Takeaways

- **Minimum Cut as a Pseudo-Boolean Compiler**: Identifying $x_v = [v \in V_S] \in \{0, 1\}$ ($x_S = 1, x_T = 0$) compiles every directed edge $(u \xrightarrow{c} v)$ into the quadratic cut monomial $c \cdot x_u(1 - x_v)$.
- **Optimistic Baseline Accounting (`先拿后退`)**: Any profit maximization $\max \sum_{u} w_u x_u$ converts into a non-negative minimum cut via $\sum_{w_u > 0} w_u - \text{MinCut}(S, T)$, where severing $S \xrightarrow{w_u} u$ forfeits a pre-claimed reward and severing $v \xrightarrow{|w_v|} T$ pays an incurred cost.
- **Picard's Maximum-Weight Closure Theorem (1976)**: Compiling $x_u = 1 \implies x_v = 1$ as $u \xrightarrow{+\infty} v$ establishes an exact bijection between closed subsets $C \subseteq U$ and finite-capacity $(S, T)$-cuts, with $S_{\min} \setminus \{S\}$ constructively recovering the unique minimum-cardinality optimal closure.
- **Causal Cycle Pruning (`FM-09`)**: When prerequisites represent sequential physical unlocking (`Semantics B`), Kahn's topological BFS on $G_{\text{pre}}$ must precede Dinic to eliminate both deadlocked cycles and their acyclic causal descendants.

### Bridge to Chapter 10: From One-Sided Closure to All-$S$ / All-$T$ Synergy Hubs and General Submodular Potentials

In this chapter, every project reward $+w_u$ lived on a **single side** of the cut ($V_S$), and every dependency $x_u = 1 \implies x_v = 1$ pointed in one direction.

What happens when a problem grants bonuses on **both sides** of the partition simultaneously—for instance, in **`[国家集训队] 文理分科` (`Luogu P4313`)** or **`CF 311 E — Biologist`**, where a group of students $A \subseteq U$ earns a synergy bonus $B_A > 0$ if **all** of them choose Arts ($x_i = 1$ for all $i \in A$, an **All-$S$ clause** $\prod_{i \in A} x_i$) AND another bonus $B'_A > 0$ if **all** of them choose Science ($x_i = 0$ for all $i \in A$, an **All-$T$ clause** $\prod_{i \in A} (1 - x_i)$)? And what if two variables $x_i, x_j \in \{0, 1\}$ interact via a general $2 \times 2$ payoff matrix $\begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix}$ without creating auxiliary vertices?

In **Chapter 10**, we generalize Picard's closure network to **High-Arity All-$S$ / All-$T$ Synergy Hubs**, derive Hu Botao's **Symmetric Vertex-Edge Merging (`合并点边法`)**, and lays the foundation for the **Kolmogorov–Zabih Submodularity Theorem ($A + D \le B + C$)** and **Bipartite Variable Inversion (`二部グラフの片側反転`)**.
